issues.legal_issue: A written family arrangement that itself divides immovable property and relinquishes inherited rights must be registered, and an unregistered, unstamped instrument cannot be admitted to prove the primary fact of partition.
material_facts: The properties were the deceased father's self-acquired properties, and he remained their owner when the alleged earlier division was said to have occurred.
After his death, his widow, sons, and daughters inherited interests in the properties.
A later written document divided the properties between the two sons, thereby relinquishing the other heirs' interests.
The document was unregistered and insufficiently stamped, and it was offered in a civil property suit as evidence of the partition.
issues.conclusion: The document was a family settlement itself, not merely a memorandum of an already completed settlement. It required compulsory registration and, being unregistered and unstamped, was inadmissible to prove the primary purpose of partition.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, a document that creates or extinguishes rights in immovable property through a family arrangement requires registration; Section 49 bars an unregistered document from proving the transaction for which registration is required. Under Section 35 of the Indian Stamp Act, an unstamped instrument is inadmissible. Kale v. Deputy Director of Consolidation (1976) 3 SCC 119 distinguishes a written instrument effecting a family arrangement from a memorandum recording an arrangement already made. Yellapu Uma Maheswari v. Buddha Jagadheeswararao (2015) 16 SCC 787 holds that the document's substance and terms, rather than its label or the parties' pleadings, determine its admissibility.

rule.if: property_suit_relying_on_partition_document and document_effects_property_division and document_relinquishes_inherited_interests and not document_registerable_formalities_met

predicates.property_suit_relying_on_partition_docum: A party in a civil property suit relied on a written instrument as evidence of a partition.
predicates.document_effects_property_division: The instrument itself set out and effected the division of immovable property rather than merely recording a division already completed.
predicates.document_relinquishes_inherited_interest: The division in the instrument relinquished interests held by other heirs in the property.
predicates.document_registerable_formalities_met: The instrument met the formal requirements for registration and stamping.

issues.definition: When a party relies on an instrument in a civil property suit, and the instrument itself divides property and relinquishes inherited interests without meeting the required formalities, the instrument cannot prove the primary partition.

issues.legal_issue: An unregistered family-settlement instrument may be used for a collateral purpose in a partition-related proceeding only after it is impounded and the required stamp duty and penalty are paid.
material_facts: The document was unregistered and unstamped.
The document was offered in a property dispute, and the Court considered whether it could be used for a purpose collateral to proving the division of property by metes and bounds.
issues.conclusion: The document could be admitted for a collateral purpose, subject to being impounded and payment of stamp duty and penalty, and subject to proof and relevance.
issues.legal_principle: Section 49 of the Registration Act prevents an unregistered instrument from proving the primary transaction requiring registration, but it may be considered for a collateral purpose, such as severance of title or the nature of possession, rather than division by metes and bounds. Under Section 35 of the Indian Stamp Act, an unstamped instrument cannot be admitted even for a collateral purpose until it is impounded and the required duty and penalty are paid. Yellapu Uma Maheswari v. Buddha Jagadheeswararao (2015) 16 SCC 787, applying Chinnappareddigari Peda Mutyala Reddy v. Chinnappareddigari Venkata Reddy, AIR 1969 AP 242, states these limits.

rule.if: partition_related_property_proceeding and unregistered_instrument and unstamped_instrument and collateral_use_sought

predicates.partition_related_property_proceeding: The proceeding concerns rights or possession arising from a claimed partition of property.
predicates.unregistered_instrument: The instrument has not been registered despite being one that requires registration.
predicates.unstamped_instrument: The instrument has not been duly stamped.
predicates.collateral_use_sought: The party seeks to use the instrument for a purpose other than proving the primary division of property by metes and bounds.

issues.definition: In a partition-related property proceeding, an unregistered and unstamped instrument sought for a collateral purpose may be used after impounding and stamp compliance.
